newsitem.title: USA: World Bank unveils restructuring plan.
newsitem.headline: World Bank unveils restructuring plan.

text.p: The World Bank on Thursday unveiled a proposed restructuring of the lending institution that will give new muscle to front line development operations at a cost of as much as $570 million over two years.

Officials said that when the effort is completed, the Bank will be about about the same size as it is today but probably with fewer employees and greater operational skill in helping countries in developing banking and social sectors.
At the same time, the bank will undergo a vast improvement in how it manages knowledge, allowing poor countries to more easily tap into information sources using the latest technology.

The proposal, which must be given the green light by the Bank's executive board, is likely to run into tough questioning by some wealthy countries that in the past have accused it of being inefficient with a bloated bureaucracy.

"The goal of this whole exercise is to bring our budget back to where it is now (in two years) but with a very different set of allocations and priorities," an official said, adding: "We do not see this as an expansion budget."
A U.S. Treasury Department spokeswoman said that they had received a copy of the proposal, called the "Strategic Compact," and were studying it.
While some 500 to 700 employees could be laid off at a cost of $150 million as its back office operations are pared down, the bank would also be hiring to beef up its direct development efforts.
The Bank said $170 million of the cost would come from internal savings and redeployment while the remaining $250 million would require an increase in budget over two years.

It estimated in inflation adjusted terms, the Bank will have only a 3.0 percent increase in its budget when the restructuring is completed in fiscal 1999 ending June 30. The bank's current annual budget is about $1.1 billion.
The new plan is the brain-child of World Bank President James Wolfensohn, who took over the institution a year and a half go and has criticised it for being inflexible in a rapidly changing world.

The Bank, which has undergone a number of downsizings and restruturing in recent years, has found that staff operations at the project level have been short-changed and employees are hard-pressed to handle their responsibilities.
The goal is to rebuild the staffs of those who actually make and administer the loans and loan programmes, while cutting back on back office support people, the bank said.
